D.J. Paris sits down with Justin Helmus, a top 1% producer in Tampa Bay and an NAR 30 Under 30 honoree who has sold the highest-priced condo on Clearwater Beach and the highest-priced home in Belleair for their years. They cover why he ignored the advice to let business come to him, how he wins luxury and investor clients, and the plan he would follow in a first 12 months.

What you’ll learn

  • Know the market better than anyone. At 25, Justin knew he couldn’t out-relationship agents with decades in town, so he learned every segment of the market and every detail of a property. (05:57)
  • Handwritten notes beat more social posts. He writes and hand delivers notes to prospective buyers and other luxury agents, and looks ahead at life events like a graduation. (13:54)
  • Go where your ideal clients are. He sat at the table nearest the door of a copy shop with old MLS sheets, and says it led to five to 10 deals. (29:04)
  • Build a team around a target listing. For a home he wants, he sends a handwritten note, then asks a neighbor and a mutual friend to put in a good word. (32:00)
  • Study the market every day. Justin spends at least an hour a day on what’s going on, because if he doesn’t, his competition is. (26:38)

“I mean, handwritten notes, bar none, is the best use of your time, in my opinion.”

Watch this interview on YouTube.

Live from Zillow Unlock 2026 in Las Vegas, D.J. Paris sits down with Mischa Fisher, Chief Economist at Zillow. They cover why some markets are rising while others cool, the one number agents should check every month, how to talk to buyers about today’s rates, and what to plan for before spring 2027.

What you’ll learn

  • Check one number a month. Mischa’s pick is the change in Zillow’s home values, because it shows the balance of supply and demand better than sold prices or price cuts. Right now home values are rising, but by less than inflation. (10:53)
  • Buyers have more choice than they’ve had in years. Inventory has grown for more than 30 months in a row in most markets. (16:14)
  • Pricing is where listings are won or lost. Well-priced listings with full exposure are selling in the normal amount of time. Get the strategy wrong and the listing lingers. (24:13)
  • Watch your local rental market. The gap between renting and owning has been shrinking, and as it shrinks, more renters turn into buyers. (29:54)
  • Get ready for volatility. If rates drop faster than expected, competition ramps up quickly. Reconnect with your sphere now, not when it happens. (31:15)

“If you’re getting that listing strategy wrong, then you’re looking at lingering for months and you’re in the price cut purgatory.”

Watch this interview on YouTube.

Kim Rittberg, a speaking and video coach for real estate agents and founders, and a former TV producer and media executive who worked at Netflix, joins Keeping It Real for a short solo episode on AI. She explains why generic AI content makes agents look the same, and how to use AI and video to show clients who you are.

What you’ll learn

  • AI exposes generic content. If your posts are something anyone with an AI account could make, or just what your brokerage hands you, they won’t help clients get to know or trust you. (04:21)
  • Tell AI about yourself. Give it your audience, your area and what sets you apart, such as a finance background, a love of interior design or strong negotiating, so the scripts are for you and not for anybody. (05:39)
  • Redline the draft like a contract. Change anything that doesn’t sound like you or doesn’t show you as the expert, and skip any script another agent in your area could also make. (06:36)
  • Win the first two seconds. Every video needs a compelling opening, because that moment either sinks the content or makes it work. (07:45)
  • Your speaking skills set you apart. Because everyone else is making the same kind of content, showing up on video makes you more competitive and more compelling. (08:51)

“So the one thing that AI cannot copy right now is you. You being uniquely charming, you being uniquely insightful, you having decades of experience, maybe one year, maybe 20 years of experience, that is what AI can’t copy.”

Sarah Maslowski, a real estate agent who says she has closed over $140 million in real estate directly from YouTube with no paid ads and no cold calling, hosts this solo episode of The YouTube Lab on Keeping It Real. She takes on the fear that stops most agents before they press record, and answers the most common excuses one by one.

What you’ll learn

  • Successful channels aren’t polished. The agents getting leads and closings from YouTube were regular agents talking about life in their area, not TV hosts. Sarah realized she only had to show up as herself and give people the information they were looking for. (04:34)
  • Editing hides the stumbles. You can stop, fumble a sentence and start again while filming, and a good editor leaves one clean, confident thought. (05:59)
  • Comfort comes from doing it. Sarah says nobody is comfortable on camera at first. A teleprompter app can take the pressure off if going off the cuff feels terrifying. (06:49)
  • Your market is your content. The best neighborhoods, the commute and what surprises people about moving there are questions you have answered for clients for years. (08:28)
  • There is room for you. Even with a dozen agents making videos about her market, Sarah says they are all getting business, and that YouTube produces the most leads of the platforms agents use. (09:02)

“Nobody is comfortable on camera at first. Nobody. Comfort comes from doing it, not from waiting until you feel ready.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Anna Kara, a loan officer who started as a receptionist and built her own mortgage company by age 20, and who works with borrowers in all 50 states. They cover how to talk to buyers who want to wait for lower rates, why the monthly payment matters more than the rate, how she helps self-employed borrowers, and how to build a brand people remember.

What you’ll learn

  • Waiting for lower rates creates competition. Anna says a house with five competing buyers today can draw 20 or 30 when rates drop, and she has seen 61 offers on one transaction. The rate can change later, but the purchase price can’t. (21:54)
  • Show the payment, not just the rate. When she locks a rate she gives buyers six or seven options with costs and payments side by side, so they can see when paying $12,000 up front doesn’t make sense. (17:38)
  • Self-employed borrowers are often turned down because of the filing. Anna works with the borrower’s CPA so allowable add-backs aren’t lost, and she has bank statement and asset depletion programs when tax returns aren’t enough. (09:25)
  • Say “here’s the reality,” not “I’ll fix this.” After a deal stalled for weeks while a borrower’s accounts were shut down, Anna changed how she talks to clients: lay out the situation and what she can do, then let them decide. (35:34)
  • Build your brand on being real. Anna gives information and never pitches. She says people remember the person they feel they know when they are ready to buy, and that authenticity and consistency matter most. (26:48)

“And if they make sense, they make sense. Numbers don’t lie at the end of the day.”

Anna Kara (at 14:42)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this month’s Better Your Business With Ben, D.J. Paris sits down with Ben Lalez, who leads the Ben Lalez Team, a Chicago team of about 30 agents. Ben explains why his team calls the fourth quarter “separation season,” why the next 90 days are about planting seeds for 2027, and how to find the activities that actually produced your past deals.

What you’ll learn

  • Q4 is when agents separate themselves. Many agents take their foot off the gas, and for the next two or three months the work won’t show a visible result. Ben says the agents who push through the uncomfortable basics are the ones who plant the seeds for Q1. (04:13)
  • Do the scary thing, then leave people behind. Each time you do something that scares you, like picking up the phone, you pass the agents who didn’t. Ben says he has trained himself to get excited when something scares him. (08:50)
  • Run an autopsy on your past deals. List where each transaction came from, then ask why that person referred you and what triggered it. Pick the activities you can repeat, not the lucky ones, and do those for the next 90 days. (13:40)
  • “I already have an agent” is not a no. Ben cites a National Association of REALTORS study and says 85% of agents never contact their client after the sale. His line: “I want to be your backup agent,” then send value every month. (16:01)
  • Add new people to your database. Ben says only 2.8% of homes in America sold last year, so a smaller share of your sphere will need you in the next 12 months. Ask for referrals, and go meet new people. (18:28)

“I want to be your backup agent in case anything ever happens. And then you just consistently send value to them every month and wait five years and see what happens.”

Ben Lalez (at 17:41)

In this Monday Market Minute, D.J. Paris sits down with Carrie McCormick, who leads the Carrie McCormick Luxury Group at @properties Christie’s International Real Estate in Chicago. They cover how to answer “how’s the market?”, what luxury buyers want right now, how to price a listing this fall, and how clients are using AI to challenge agents.

What you’ll learn

  • Answer “how’s the market?” with a question. Each neighborhood, building, housing stock and price point performs differently, so Carrie asks which market and which segment the person means. She says that specific answer builds credibility. (07:35)
  • Luxury buyers are discerning. Carrie lists location, architecture, privacy, views, land, condition and a home that feels special as what matters to buyers around $5 million. Most want plug and play, because time is their most valuable resource. (09:29)
  • Don’t chase the market this fall. The first few weeks on the market are when everyone is watching, so Carrie says to watch pricing, activity and marketing in the first two weeks. Pricing, presentation and positioning matter most. (14:43)
  • AI is a fact-checker, not a replacement. Clients now arrive saying “my chat said this,” so Carrie says agents have to know their information cold. She uses AI as a coach and always double checks it. (18:44)
  • Be there when they decide. Carrie stays away from automated touch points because she wants the human touch, and she uses a Nordstrom shoe department story to explain why: you want to be the person standing there when the client is ready. (29:24)

“If the house is sitting on the market more than 120 days, they see that as a negotiating strategy. So the buyers have become so intuitive into what this market is.”

Carrie McCormick (at 15:50)

D.J. Paris sits down with Brenton Miebach of Southwest Florida Lifestyle Living with eXp Realty in Cape Coral, Florida, a former Army National Guard military police officer who built his business from scratch in Orlando and then again in Cape Coral. They cover buying internet leads, learning a market fast, the AI system he built in Claude, and how a Facebook page grew from about 150 followers to nearly 3,000 in about 10 days.

What you’ll learn

  • Learn the market before you prospect. In his first 30 days in Cape Coral, Brenton drove around finding the hospitals and schools and talked to local people so he could navigate the area. (06:48)
  • Be first on paid leads. Brenton spent about $3,000 a month on Realtor.com leads in Orlando and up to about $7,000 a month on Zillow leads in Southwest Florida. He bought an Apple Watch so he could call leads the moment they came in. (11:17)
  • Keep the information in front of you on cold calls. He never tries to bluff, and keeps the MLS and Google Maps open so he can talk about the house two doors down that sold four months ago. (18:05)
  • Build AI skills your team can share. Brenton built a showing packet skill that schedules showings, pulls MLS and county data, and produces a printable PDF, so every agent on his team prepares the same way. (48:34)
  • Use AI to make local history content. He photographed a book about Cape Coral, had Claude turn it into video ideas and colorized old photos, and the videos drew more than 100,000 views. (1:01:44)

“The internet leads for me weren’t an easy button. The internet leads for me were a way for me to break into a market and actually get deals done…”

Paris sits down with Bill Melnick, a luxury agent with Harney Real Estate in Litchfield County, Connecticut, who spent 28 years at Ralph Lauren and rose to chief merchandising officer before switching careers. They cover how a lifestyle-merchandising mindset shapes his listings, how he sold Ivan Lendl’s estate for a county-record $12 million, and why second-primary buyers are changing his market.

What you’ll learn

  • Sell the lifestyle, not just the house. Bill says luxury buyers look for 360 degrees of lifestyle: the location, the cachet, the home and the view. His job is to present all of it in a cohesive way. (05:58)
  • Edit before you photograph. Staging is mostly editing. Remove clutter and anything that becomes visual pollution so buyers can picture their own things in the space. (07:34)
  • Price is more than square footage. In his market, lakefront, big mountain views and pools can add real money, and so can usable acreage and conservation land next door. Bill calls it a much more complicated equation. (11:36)
  • At the top end, you find the buyer. On the Lendl estate, Bill partnered with his broker and called top agents in nearby markets and New York City. He says a lot of agents don’t understand that in luxury you often have to find the buyer for the listing. (19:43)
  • Go easy on AI for client messages. Bill uses AI for research and for drafting brochure copy that he edits, but he says answering every email with it is a turn-off for buyers and other agents. (42:07)

“…a lot of agents don’t understand about luxury is a lot of times you got to find the buyer for the listing agent.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Alex Maldonado, a Los Angeles agent with Circle Real Estate who serves South LA, East LA, Northeast LA and Long Beach, works with first-time and first-generation buyers in English and Spanish, and also runs Maldonado Marketing. They cover how to close the gap when a buyer has the down payment but not the closing costs, how to keep an offer with credits competitive, and how Alex generates leads.

What you’ll learn

  • Cover closing costs with credits. Alex works with a lender who offers lender credits and writes seller credits into the contract. If the buyer has the 3.5% down payment, or can get it from family, he says he can usually get them to ownership. (08:26)
  • Make the offer strong in other ways. To offset credits, Alex builds them into the price, offers 3% earnest money and uses a lender that can close in 21 days, because sellers care about their net and speed. (15:53)
  • Break bad news slowly. When a buyer fell in love with a neighborhood she couldn’t afford, Alex sent her recent closing prices so she could judge for herself, and explained that many of the listings were cash-only. (13:41)
  • Know your local assistance programs. Alex explains city and county down payment assistance as a way to get in the door and start building wealth, in exchange for giving up a share of the appreciation. (19:10)

In this YouTube Lab episode, Sarah Maslowski of Keypoint Homes Group in Georgia shares how she thinks about titles and thumbnails. She says she has closed over $150 million in real estate from YouTube with no paid ads and no cold calling, and she walks through the title mistakes agents make, how to research better titles and her full thumbnail system.

What you’ll learn

  • A title has one job. It is not to describe the video. It is to make someone curious enough to click. (04:30)
  • Use AI for title ideas. Drop your first title into an AI tool and ask for 10 more clickable versions, then narrow it to two or three. (07:04)
  • Let YouTube test it. The built-in A/B test shows which title or thumbnail viewers actually click, so you stop guessing. (07:31)
  • Treat the thumbnail like a magazine cover. Use a big face with a real expression, a background that shows the topic, consistent fonts and colors, and no more than three to five words. (09:05)
  • Keep the editor and thumbnail designer separate. The skills are different, and in her experience thumbnails from video editors have underperformed. (15:14)

“Titles and thumbnails are the front door of your YouTube channel.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this month’s Learning With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Austin Clarence, a mortgage loan officer and investor financing specialist at Nexa Mortgage. They cover how oil prices and the Fed feed into mortgage rates, why home values have kept rising, and loan programs agents can bring to doctors, veterans and self-employed buyers.

What you’ll learn

  • Oil prices reach mortgage rates. Oil touches trucking, shipping and manufacturing, so it shows up in inflation. With crude down from about $120 to $69 a barrel, Austin expects relief to reach rates over the coming months. (06:53)
  • Home values kept rising. Even with elevated rates, Austin points to national appreciation, which is a good talking point for buyers deciding whether to wait. (15:25)
  • Ask buyers what they do for work. Doctor loans can mean no down payment and no PMI, and they can be more forgiving of student loans. (21:07)
  • VA loans are easier to qualify for. He says FHA loans max out at a 56% debt-to-income ratio at every lender, while a VA loan can go up to 70% with residual income. (26:48)
  • Self-employed buyers have options. An FHA program with 3.5% down lets buyers prepare their own profit and loss statement instead of waiting on tax returns. (32:28)

“Oil is really involved with everything with trucking, shipping, manufacturing. It’s not just filling up at the pump. It’s everything that gets to the grocery store, everything that you’re purchasing online, the Amazon driver.”

Austin Clarence (at 07:46)
